demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: 'Talks or photos about snakes' is not clinically coherent as a trigger for PTSD centered on the unexpected death of a loved one unless the death involved snakes, which is not indicated. It appears trauma-unrelated and weakly connected to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' implies perceived preventability and personal responsibility during the death event. That can occur, but it is not supported by the rest of the profile, which lacks any memory or trigger content suggesting direct involvement in the loved one's death.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: 'Starting new friendships or relationships' as an avoided strategy is a poor fit for a married 28-year-old male whose trauma is bereavement, and it is not well linked to the stated triggers/appraisals. It suggests interpersonal avoidance without supporting appraisals such as mistrust, fear of loss, or social threat.

vignette: Carlos had always taken pride in his work as a prison guard, but that was before his younger brother, Alex, was killed in a senseless act of violence. It had been six months since the funeral, and Carlos still couldn't shake off the feeling of detachment that had settled over him like a shroud. He would find himself zoning out in the middle of conversations, or feeling like he was watching himself go through the motions of his daily routine from outside his body. It started with little things - seeing a news report about another senseless killing, hearing someone talk about losing a loved one, and suddenly Carlos would feel like he was floating above the ground. He'd try to shake off the dissociative feeling by covering his face with his hands, as if physical contact could anchor him back in reality. But it wasn't just the media or conversations that triggered these episodes - anything that reminded him of Alex, from the smell of his cologne to the sound of his favorite song, would send Carlos spiraling. As time went on, Carlos began to notice a pattern: whenever he felt himself starting to detach, he'd pick arguments with his wife or create drama at work. It was as if he needed the adrenaline rush of conflict to distract him from the crushing grief that threatened to overwhelm him. He knew it wasn't healthy, but he couldn't seem to stop himself - and besides, what did it matter? He had no future, no happiness left in his life anyway. The more Carlos struggled with these feelings, the more convinced he became that he was somehow responsible for Alex's death. If only he'd been there, if only he'd been able to protect him... The weight of this self-blame crushed Carlos, making it harder and harder for him to face the world outside his home. He started avoiding anything that reminded him of Alex - photos, mementos, even certain streets they used to walk down together. But avoidance only seemed to make things worse: the more Carlos hid from his grief, the more he felt like he was losing himself. He'd catch glimpses of himself in mirrors or windows and barely recognize the person staring back. And yet, every time he tried to confront these feelings head-on, he'd feel that familiar sense of detachment creeping back in - as if his own mind was conspiring against him. Carlos's wife had been patient with him so far, but he could see the strain starting to show on her face. She didn't understand why he couldn't just "get over it" already - after all, hadn't they both lost Alex? But for Carlos, there was no "getting over" this kind of pain. It was as if he'd been sentenced to a life term in his own private prison, with no parole in sight. It was the look on his wife's face that finally brought Carlos to seek help - the same look he saw every time he walked out the door to go to work, feeling like a shadow of the man he used to be. He didn't know what he hoped for from therapy, but he knew he couldn't keep living like this. The thought of facing his grief head-on was terrifying, but it was also the only way Carlos could see to start rebuilding himself - and maybe, just maybe, find a way out of the darkness that had consumed him.
